en: The Sūtra on the Five Things Without Reciprocity, translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, together with a thousand [monks].

Accompanied by two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, there was at that time a brahmin living in the kingdom of Rājagṛha who heard that the people of Śrāvastī were compassionate, filial, and obedient; that they honored the sutras and cultivated the Way, and made offerings to the Triple Gem. He then traveled to the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
He saw the father and son plowing a field when a venomous snake bit and killed the son.
The father continued to plow as before; he neither looked at his son nor wept.
A brahmin asked him:
"Whose son is this child? The plowman replied, "He is my son."
The brahmin said,
"This son of yours— why does he not weep, but instead continues to plow as before? The man replied:
"Human life ends in death; things that flourish end in decay; the good receive their reward, and the wicked meet their retribution. What can sorrow, lamentation, and weeping accomplish?"
"If one does not provide food or drink, what benefit is there for the deceased?
Now that you have entered the city, my house is at such-and-such a place; I pray you will go there and tell them:
'My son has already died.'"
"There is no need to bring food for two people.
The brahmin thought to himself:
"This man has no sense of reciprocity; though his son lies dead on the ground, he feels no grief or sorrow, yet instead demands food."
"This man is merciless; there is no one like him.
The brahmin then proceeded into the city, went to the house of the plowman, saw the mother of the deceased child, and immediately said to her:
"Your son is already dead."
The father said:
"Bring food for only one person.
Why do you not consider your son?
The child’s mother countered the brahmin with a parable, saying:
“A son is like a guest who comes to dwell in dependence upon another;
he is not turned away when he arrives, nor is he detained when he departs.”
This child was originally not summoned by me, yet he came to me of his own accord; at birth he came of his own accord, and at death he will likewise depart of his own accord.
It is not by my power that he is made to advance or retreat; he follows his own past conduct as he pursues the destiny of his rebirth.
He further said to his sister, "Your brother is already dead; why do you not weep?
The sister then spoke a parable to the brahmin:

“We brothers were like master craftsmen who entered the mountains to fell timber and bound it together to make a great raft. Having placed it upon the water, we were suddenly caught in a great wind that blew the raft apart and scattered it; carried away by the current, we were separated from one another, drifting forward and backward without looking back.”
It is the same with my younger brother; due to such karmic conditions from past lives, we were born together in one household at the same time.
Depending on the length of our lifespans, birth and death are impermanent; where there is meeting, there must be parting.
"My younger brother's life has come to an end; each must follow his own path.
When impermanence confronts one, one follows the results of one's own past actions, and no one can save another.
He then spoke to the deceased's wife:
“Your husband has already died; why do you not weep?
The wife again spoke a parable for the brahmin, saying:
“We, husband and wife, have met through causes and conditions for but a brief moment.”
It is like birds that, at evening, perch together to roost upon a tall tree; as dawn approaches, they rise early and each flies away to seek food and drink.
They come together when there is a cause for doing so, and they separate when there is no such cause.
We, husband and wife, are likewise so; our going and staying, our advancing and halting, are not by our own power.
When impermanence arrives, we must follow our respective karmic destinies and cannot save one another.
He further said to his servant, "Your master's son has died; why do you not weep?
The servant then spoke a parable:
"My master has met with his karmic conditions.
I am like a calf following a great bull;
when people slaughter the great bull, the calf stands by its side, unable to save it."
"Life, being impermanent, cannot be saved; what use is it to grieve, worry, or weep? It will bring no benefit.
Upon hearing this, the Brahmin’s mind was bewildered and his vision grew dark; he could not distinguish east from west, thinking:

"I heard that the people of this country are filial, devoted to the Way, and serve the Triple Gem. That is why I traveled from afar wishing to study and learn. Yet, having received no favorable response, I have instead encountered these five people who lack any sense of reciprocity."
"I have toiled my body and exhausted my mind to come this far, yet it has been of no benefit at all.
He then asked the traveler, "Where is the Buddha?"
"I wish to go and ask him about it.
The traveler replied,
"He is nearby, at the Jetavana Monastery."

The brahmin immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet in salutation, and withdrew to sit to one side; he sat with a sorrowful air, head bowed low, remaining silent and saying nothing.
The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, said to the brahmin:
"Why do you lower your head,
sorrowful and unhappy?"
The brahmin said to the Buddha, “My wishes have not been fulfilled; they contradict my original intention, and for this reason I am sorrowful and anxious.
The Buddha asked:
"What have you lost that you are so sorrowful and unhappy?
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have come from the kingdom of Rājagṛha. Hearing that the people of this country are filial and obedient, and that they revere and honor the Triple Gem, I have come from afar wishing to study."
"Having come here, I see these five people who lack any sense of reciprocity; therefore, I am sorrowful and find no joy.
The Buddha asked, "What do you mean by 'those who lack reciprocity'?"
The brahmin said to the Buddha:

"I saw a father and son plowing the earth and sowing seeds; the son died on the ground, yet the father felt no grief and instead went about seeking food, even going so far as to preach the matter of impermanence to me."
"His mother, his wife, his sisters, and his slaves—none of them feel any sorrow or anxiety.
This is what is meant by being a great rebel, devoid of gratitude and reciprocity.
The Buddha said:
"It is not so; it is not as you say.
These five men were most loyal and returned their debt of gratitude. Knowing that life is impermanent, they are beyond the reach of sorrow and grief.
Even the sages of antiquity could not avoid this affliction, let alone ordinary people. What benefit do great wailing and small weeping bring to the deceased?"

Ordinary people of the world have wandered through birth and death for countless kalpas; their spirits transmigrate without ceasing, dying and being born again like the turning of a wheel that never rests.
"To turn one's back on death and face life is not something that sorrow can reach.
Upon hearing this, the brahmin’s mind was opened and his understanding clarified; he was no longer burdened by grief or distress, thinking:
"I have heard the Buddha’s teaching, which is like recovering from an illness, like a blind man regaining his sight, or like encountering light in the darkness."
Thereupon, the brahmin immediately attained the fruit of the Path.
[He realized that] "All death is not a cause for weeping; I wish to invite the Buddha and the Sangha on behalf of the deceased to offer incense and make offerings, and to recite the scriptures."
"To be able to pay homage every day and further to offer worship with a sincere mind to the Triple Gem is the most essential thing.
Thereupon, the Brahmin bowed his head in prostration, received these instructions, and departed.
The Sūtra on the Five Things That Cannot Be Reciprocated Spoken by the Buddha.
